questions.question: Why can't a Filter simply call something like `response.getBody()` after `chain.doFilter()` to read what the controller returned?
options: The body is available, but only through `response.getHeader("Body")` after the response is committed
The body is stored in the request object, so the Filter must call `request.getAttribute("body")` instead
`HttpServletResponse` is a destination that data is written into via `getWriter()`/`getOutputStream()`, not an object that keeps the full body for later reading
The body exists only inside the controller method's stack frame and is destroyed before the Filter resumes
questions.explanation: The controller (via Spring MVC) writes bytes into the response's writer/output stream and they move on towards the client; the plain response does not retain them as a readable body. To inspect or replace the body later you must pass a wrapper such as `ContentCachingResponseWrapper` down the chain. The body is not stored in request attributes or headers.

questions.question: This Filter (from the lecture code) is registered for all URLs. A client sends `POST /api/students` WITHOUT any `token` header. What happens?
options: The client gets 401 with the JSON message, and the controller is never invoked
A `NullPointerException` occurs at `token.equals("12345")`, giving a 500 response
The client gets 401, but the controller still runs and its JSON is appended after the message
The 401 is ignored because the status can only be set by the controller, so the client gets 200
questions.explanation: `token == null` is true, so `||` short-circuits and `equals` is never called (no NPE). The Filter writes the 401 JSON response and returns without calling `filterChain.doFilter()`, so the request never reaches the DispatcherServlet or the controller. Returning without calling the chain means 'stop processing here'.

questions.question: A teammate adds a Filter that reads the whole JSON body with `request.getReader()` and logs it, then calls `chain.doFilter(request, response)`. Now every `@PostMapping` with `@RequestBody Student` fails with "Required request body is missing". What is the correct fix?
options: Switch the Filter from `getReader()` to `getInputStream()`, since that stream can be read independently of the reader
Call `reader.reset()` after logging so the stream goes back to position zero for Spring MVC
Move the Filter to a lower order so it runs after the DispatcherServlet has already parsed the body
Read the bytes once, cache them, and pass down a custom `HttpServletRequestWrapper` whose `getInputStream()`/`getReader()` return fresh streams over the cached bytes
questions.explanation: The body is a one-way network stream; once the Filter consumes it, nothing remains for Jackson. The standard fix is to cache the bytes and hand downstream code a wrapper that returns a new `ByteArrayInputStream` (starting at position 0) every time. `getReader()` and `getInputStream()` are two views of the same body, so switching between them does not help, and the container's reader cannot be rewound to replay network bytes.

questions.question: The controller returns `{"name":"Aditya"}` with status 200. What does the client receive with this Filter in place?
options: Status 200 with `{"name":"Aditya"}`, because the wrapper forwards writes to the real response as they happen
An empty body, because the bytes stay cached inside the wrapper and `copyBodyToResponse()` is never called
Status 500, because `getContentAsByteArray()` throws once the response has been committed
The body twice, because the controller writes to both the wrapper and the original response
questions.explanation: `ContentCachingResponseWrapper` caches everything written to its writer/output stream and does not forward it to the real response until `copyBodyToResponse()` is called. Omitting that call means the client gets no body (the log line still prints the size). This is why the notes call `copyBodyToResponse()` an essential final step.

questions.question: `RequestLoggingFilter` is annotated with `@Component`, and a `@Configuration` class also exposes a `FilterRegistrationBean` that calls `setFilter(new RequestLoggingFilter())` with `addUrlPatterns("/api/*")`. Each `/api/students` request is logged twice. Why?
options: `FilterRegistrationBean` always invokes its filter once for the request and once for the response
Spring Boot runs a Filter once per URL pattern, and `/api/*` counts as two patterns
Two separate registrations exist: the `@Component` bean (mapped broadly to `/*`) and the manual registration of a second instance
`@Component` filters are run once by the servlet container and again by the DispatcherServlet
questions.explanation: Spring Boot auto-registers a `Filter` bean (mapped to `/*`), and the `FilterRegistrationBean` registers another instance created with `new`. Both match `/api/students`, so the logic runs twice. Pick one strategy: drop `@Component` when you register the filter manually.

questions.question: How does Spring's `OncePerRequestFilter` avoid running `doFilterInternal()` twice for the same request dispatch?
options: It stores an 'already filtered' request attribute and, if it is present, passes the request down the chain without calling `doFilterInternal()` again
It keeps a static `Set` of request URIs it has already processed and skips repeated URIs
It registers itself with order `Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE`, which makes the container call it only once
It caches the request body, so a second invocation finds no data and returns immediately
questions.explanation: `OncePerRequestFilter.doFilter()` checks for a request attribute (the filter name plus `.FILTERED`). If the attribute is set it skips `doFilterInternal()`; otherwise it sets it and runs the logic. A URI-based static set would wrongly skip later, separate requests to the same URL, and ordering has nothing to do with how many times a filter runs.

questions.question: This filter is registered for all URLs. A client calls `GET /hello`. What is the bug?
options: It fails to compile, because the statement after the `if` block is unreachable
`/hello` is skipped completely: nothing is printed and the chain runs once, as intended
The `if` branch throws `IllegalStateException` immediately, so nothing is printed and `/hello` returns 500 before reaching the controller
Without a `return` in the `if` block, `/hello` is passed down the chain, then "Dummy filter called" is printed, and the chain is invoked a second time
questions.explanation: Because the `if` block does not `return`, execution falls through after the first `filterChain.doFilter()`. So the non-API request is processed downstream, the message is printed anyway, and the request is sent down the chain again (duplicate processing on an already-written response). The code compiles fine: a statement after an `if` is never unreachable. The fix is `filterChain.doFilter(...); return;`, as in the notes' `ApiFilter`.

questions.question: The lecture's `FilterConfig` registers `DummyFilter` like this, intending it to cover both `/api/students` and `/admin/users`. What actually happens?
options: It works as intended, because Spring Boot splits the string on commas and trims each pattern
The whole string is treated as ONE URL pattern, so the filter matches neither `/api/students` nor `/admin/users`; the patterns must be passed as separate arguments
Only the first pattern `/api/*` is registered and the text after the comma is silently dropped
The application fails to start because `addUrlPatterns` accepts exactly one pattern per call
questions.explanation: `addUrlPatterns(String... urlPatterns)` is varargs: each argument is one pattern, and nothing splits on commas. The single string "/api/*, /admin/*" (space included) is one odd pattern that real request paths don't match. The correct call is `addUrlPatterns("/api/*", "/admin/*")`, as shown in the notes.

questions.question: A Filter calls `httpResponse.setHeader("X-Processing-Time", ...)` AFTER `chain.doFilter()`. For small responses the header sometimes appears, but for large JSON responses it is usually missing. What explains this?
options: Downstream code wrote and flushed enough data to commit the response, so status and headers were already sent; later header changes are ignored
`setHeader()` after `chain.doFilter()` replaces the body instead of adding a header when the body is large
Headers whose names start with `X-` are dropped by Tomcat once the body exceeds a fixed size
The header must be set with `addHeader()`, because `setHeader()` is ignored once the controller has returned
questions.explanation: When the output buffer fills or is flushed, the response becomes committed: the status line and headers go to the client first. After that, header changes have no effect (check with `isCommitted()`). Headers that must always be present should be set before `chain.doFilter()`. `addHeader()` vs `setHeader()` only decides between appending and replacing values; it does not affect commit timing.

questions.question: To force `page=2`, a Filter passes down a custom `HttpServletRequestWrapper` that overrides ONLY `getParameter(String name)`. The controller has `@RequestParam int page`, and for `GET /products?page=1` it still receives 1. What is the most likely reason?
options: Query parameters are parsed by Tomcat before any Filter runs, so no wrapper can ever change them
The wrapper must also call `super.setParameter("page", "2")` in its constructor to persist the change
Spring MVC resolves request parameters through other methods such as `getParameterValues()`/`getParameterMap()`, which the wrapper did not override, so they still return the original value
`@RequestParam` reads directly from the URL string rather than from the request object
questions.explanation: Downstream components see only what the wrapper's overridden methods return. Spring's `@RequestParam` resolution uses `getParameterValues()`, and data binding uses the parameter map, so a wrapper must override `getParameter`, `getParameterValues`, `getParameterMap` and `getParameterNames` consistently. There is no `setParameter()` on the request, and wrappers do work. They just have to cover every access path.
